claims.text: The case reports acute leukaemia, bk virus infection, and cystitis haemorrhagic as reactions in a 13-year-old male patient receiving cyclosporine for graft versus host disease.
BK virus infection is listed in the cyclosporine label under warnings, with specific mention of polyoma virus-associated nephropathy (PVAN) due to BK virus infection.
Acute leukaemia is not found in the cyclosporine label warnings or adverse reactions section.
Cystitis haemorrhagic is not found in the cyclosporine label warnings or adverse reactions section.
FAERS disproportionality analysis shows a strong signal for cyclosporine and BK virus infection (PRR=94.173, ROR025=88.06, IC025=5.889), but this reflects reporting association only, not causation.
FAERS disproportionality data for cyclosporine and acute leukaemia or cystitis haemorrhagic are not available as these reactions are not among the 80 most-reported for this drug.

memo.narrative: A 13-year-old male developed acute leukaemia, BK virus infection, and haemorrhagic cystitis while on cyclosporine for GVHD, with multiple concomitant chemotherapies and immunosuppressants. BK virus infection is labeled; other reactions lack label support. Outcome was death.
open_questions: Whether acute leukaemia represents disease progression, relapse, or secondary malignancy
Role of concomitant chemotherapy (fludarabine, cytarabine) in haemorrhagic cystitis
Contribution of immunosuppression to BK virus reactivation

rules.text: Disproportionality (PRR, ROR, IC) shows a reporting association, never causation.
FAERS counts have no exposure denominator: no incidence, rate or risk estimates.
Do not rank or compare the safety of different drugs by disproportionality magnitude.
Absence of a disproportionality signal is not evidence of safety.
A reaction listed in the label does not confirm causality in this individual case.
A single case report cannot establish or confirm a signal on its own.
Number of PubMed hits is not a measure of evidence strength.
Counts may include duplicates and stimulated reporting; do not treat them as exact.
Confounding by indication and co-medication must not be ignored when attributing the reaction.
Model probabilities are population-calibrated, not certainty about this case.
No individual treatment advice or dosing recommendations for the patient.
Quoted label text must actually appear in the cited label section.
